nameStory: Shining sumac gets its common name from its glossy, waxy leaves that catch and reflect sunlight with a distinctive sheen. The scientific name 'copallinum' refers to copal, a tree resin, because this species produces a similar sticky, aromatic substance.
description: Shining sumac is a small deciduous tree or large shrub that reaches 11-18 feet tall with an equally wide, rounded crown. It's the shortest member of the sumac family you'll find in New England, earning it the nickname 'dwarf sumac.' This native plant produces clusters of small greenish flowers in summer, followed by fuzzy red berry clusters that persist into winter.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 9-21 leaflets that feel waxy and look glossy, especially on top - run your finger along them and notice how smooth and shiny they are compared to other sumacs

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Much shorter than other sumacs, typically staying under 20 feet with a dense, rounded crown that's often as wide as it is tall

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Dense, upright clusters of small red berries covered in fine hairs that feel fuzzy to touch - these clusters turn deep crimson and persist through winter

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, greenish-white flowers in dense, pyramid-shaped clusters at branch tips in mid-summer - individual flowers are tiny but the overall cluster is showy

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, gray-brown bark on young stems that becomes slightly furrowed with age, but never develops the deep ridges of larger trees

habitat: Look for shining sumac in dry, sandy soils and rocky areas throughout New England, especially along roadsides, field edges, and open woodlands. It thrives in poor soils where other trees struggle and is often found growing with pitch pine, oak, and other drought-tolerant species.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as reddish shoots in late spring, quickly developing their characteristic glossy sheen as they mature.
seasonality.summer: Greenish flower clusters appear in mid to late summer, and the waxy leaves are at their most reflective and easiest to identify.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant orange to deep red, while the fuzzy red fruit clusters ripen and become very prominent against the colorful foliage.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the plant's compact, rounded structure, with persistent red berry clusters serving as the main identifying feature.

funFact: Shining sumac's waxy leaves contain the same compounds found in poison ivy - they're in the same plant family - but this sumac is completely harmless to touch and was actually used by Native Americans to make a lemony drink from the berries!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with staghorn sumac, but shining sumac is much shorter, has glossier leaves, and lacks the fuzzy, antler-like branches that give staghorn sumac its name. Memory trick: 'shining' sumac has 'shiny' leaves, while staghorn has 'hairy' branches.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the cashew family alongside poison ivy, shining sumac is completely safe to handle. The common name 'flameleaf sumac' refers to its spectacular fall color, while 'winged sumac' comes from small wing-like extensions along the leaf stems that are sometimes present.
compareHints: Shining sumac is much smaller than staghorn sumac and lacks its fuzzy branches, while smooth sumac has completely hairless stems and duller leaves. Unlike fragrant sumac which has only 3 leaflets per leaf, shining sumac has many more leaflets and grows much taller.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Staghorn sumac is easily distinguished from its relatives by its distinctively fuzzy branches - smooth sumac has smooth branches (as the name suggests), while shining sumac has a winged stem between leaflets.
Smooth sumac differs from staghorn sumac by its hairless twigs and stems, while staghorn feels velvety-fuzzy.
Fragrant sumac is much smaller and more spreading than its tall cousins like staghorn sumac, which can reach 15-25 feet.
